The basalt’s iron content gives the wine its signature stony, almost ferrous edge, while the high quartz content in the topsoil reflects sunlight, amplifying the UV index and thickening the grapes’ skins. The wine’s salinity and citrus pith bitterness come directly from the basalt’s mineral salts and the low-vigor vines’ struggle for water in the free-draining soil.
parsed.vinification_summary: Atamisque ferments this Chardonnay in a mix of stainless steel (60%) and French oak barrels (40%), with only 20% of the oak being new. The native yeast fermentation takes place at cool temperatures (14-16°C) to preserve primary fruit, while the oak-aged portion undergoes partial malolactic fermentation (about 30%) to soften the wine’s natural acidity without erasing it. The wine is aged on its lees for 10 months with weekly bâtonnage (stirring of the lees) to build mid-palate texture, but the stirring is gentle—just enough to add creaminess without masking the basalt’s mineral bite. No fining, light filtration. The winemaker’s goal is to avoid the buttery, tropical fruit bomb that defines much of Mendoza’s Chardonnay; instead, the focus is on tension and structure, which is why the oak is used sparingly and the lees work is subtle.
